paragraphs: Online algorithms make decisions as inputs arrive, before all future information is available. Learning-augmented algorithms try to improve those decisions by predicting properties of future inputs. This paper develops a regression approach to that prediction problem, motivated by the fact that the quantities being predicted are generally real-valued.

The central idea is to design the regression loss around the performance benchmarks of the online optimization problem. This connects the predictor's training objective to the decisions its predictions will support. Standard measures of statistical prediction error do not, by themselves, provide the same connection to the online algorithm's objective.

The authors study this approach through a general online search framework encompassing problems such as ski rental, bin packing, and minimum makespan scheduling. They establish nearly tight bounds on the number of training samples needed and extend their results to the agnostic setting. The contribution is a theoretical account of learning predictions whose quality is judged through their role in online optimization.
neurips-2021-a-regression-approach-to-le.tldr: The paper develops regression losses tied to online optimization objectives and proves nearly tight sample-complexity bounds for learning useful predictions.

paragraphs: Adversarial machine learning often separates attacks that fool an already trained model from attacks that corrupt its training data. This paper connects those two settings. It shows that adversarial examples originally created to attack pretrained networks can also serve as particularly effective poisoned training examples.

The authors report that their adversarial poisoning approach is substantially more effective for secure dataset release than existing poisoning methods. They also examine what happens when the network used to craft the examples assigns them new labels. With those reassigned labels, the examples remain useful for training. This suggests that the images retain meaningful semantic information, but that the network associates that information with labels different from those a human would assign.

That result helps explain why an example that looks meaningful to a person can interfere with learning under its original label. The paper also releases ImageNet-P, a poisoned version of ImageNet, to support further study of this kind of data obfuscation and how strongly it can affect training.
neurips-2021-adversarial-examples-make-s.tldr: Adversarial examples can poison training data more effectively than dedicated poisoning methods while retaining useful information under network-assigned labels.

paragraphs: This position paper examines how a small set of influential benchmarks comes to represent progress across AI. The authors call these general benchmarks because researchers treat them as proxies for a broader collection of problems. Success on them is often interpreted as movement toward flexible systems that generalize well.

The paper focuses on the relationship between the tasks a benchmark contains and the larger ambitions attached to its results. A benchmark offers an abstraction of selected problems, while the goals of general and flexible AI extend beyond that selection. The authors investigate how benchmark design, construction, and use contribute to framing particular evaluations as broad measures of progress.

Its contribution is a critique of that framing rather than a new benchmark or learning algorithm. By examining the role these evaluations play across AI subfields, the paper aims to expose limitations in treating their scores as functionally general evidence. The central question is how much a result on an influential evaluation can support claims about AI's longer-term goals.
neurips-2021-ai-and-the-everything-in-th.tldr: This position paper questions how influential AI benchmarks become broad proxies for progress toward flexible, generalizable intelligence.

paragraphs: A generated image can look convincing while failing to depict the words that requested it. This paper studies that distinction when familiar objects and attributes appear in previously unseen combinations. It introduces compositional evaluation splits based on CUB and Oxford Flowers, targeting unseen object-color and object-shape phrases.

The authors test several recent text-to-image methods using both automatic measures and human judgments. They also introduce CLIP-R-Precision, which uses a vision-and-language model to assess correspondence between text and images. This addresses a concern with evaluation practices that reuse the same retrieval model during training and testing, potentially biasing the assessment.

Both forms of evaluation reveal a performance gap on previously unseen phrases. The results indicate that correctness relative to the requested text is especially affected, beyond purely perceptual image quality. CLIP-R-Precision also correlates better with human judgments than the commonly used metric. Together, the benchmark and evaluation method make compositional fidelity a more explicit target for assessing image generation.
neurips-2021-benchmark-for-compositional.tldr: New compositional benchmarks reveal that text-to-image models struggle with unseen attribute-object combinations, especially in matching the requested content.

paragraphs: An object detector can forget previously learned categories when it is trained on new ones without access to the original examples. Some methods address this by relying on old categories appearing, without labels, in the new training images. This paper studies the harder setting where old and new categories do not co-occur at all.

The proposed solution uses additional unlabeled images from the wild to connect the two learning stages. A sampling strategy examines responses from a model for the old categories and a pretrained model for the new categories. It selects a smaller, relevant collection from the larger image pool, creating data that can support knowledge transfer.

A dual-teacher distillation framework then trains a student using knowledge from both category-specific teachers on the selected images. Experiments on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO show significant improvements over other leading incremental detection methods under the stated absence of co-occurrence. The findings support using external unlabeled data to preserve and combine detection knowledge in this setting.
neurips-2021-bridging-non-co-occurrence-.tldr: Selected unlabeled images and two teacher models help an incremental object detector learn new categories while retaining old ones without training-data co-occurrence.

paragraphs: Learning personalized treatment effects from observational data requires outcomes from treated and untreated populations. Measuring those outcomes can be expensive, so choosing which ones to acquire matters. This paper examines how to make that choice efficiently when deep models work with high-dimensional observations.

Ordinary Bayesian active learning often selects examples where a model is uncertain. The authors identify a problem with applying this strategy directly: it can favor regions where treated and control populations do not overlap. Treatment effects are not identifiable in those regions, so high uncertainty alone does not make an outcome measurement useful for the intended causal comparison.

Causal-BALD introduces information-theoretic Bayesian acquisition functions that favor regions with overlapping support. These functions aim to direct measurement effort toward examples that inform personalized treatment effects. The authors evaluate the strategies on synthetic and semi-synthetic IHDP and CMNIST datasets and extensions designed to represent common biases and pathologies. The work connects active data acquisition to the conditions needed for meaningful treatment-effect estimation.
neurips-2021-causal-bald-deep-bayesian-a.tldr: Causal-BALD selects costly outcome measurements with attention to treated-control overlap, aiming to make personalized treatment-effect learning more sample-efficient.

paragraphs: The spatial legacy of apartheid is visible in South African neighborhoods, including segregated townships alongside wealthy gated areas. This paper introduces a public visual dataset intended to support study of how these patterns evolve. It contains 6,768 high-resolution satellite images spanning South Africa's nine provinces.

The authors construct the dataset by combining land-use polygons, geographically labeled building coordinates, and satellite imagery covering 2006–2017. An iterative process produces pixel-level labels for four categories: wealthy areas, non-wealthy areas, non-residential neighborhoods, and vacant land. These labels associate the imagery with neighborhood categories that researchers can use when examining spatial change.

The dataset also demonstrates a construction process carried out with highly constrained resources, despite the substantial annotation costs reported for smaller datasets. The paper provides examples of applications studying neighborhood evolution. Its contribution is an openly available foundation for visual analysis of spatial apartheid, alongside an account of how to build such a resource from geographic information and imagery.
neurips-2021-constructing-a-visual-datas.tldr: A public, pixel-labeled satellite-image dataset supports research into the changing spatial legacy of apartheid across South Africa.

paragraphs: This paper studies decision trees that divide a two-dimensional signal into rectangular regions and assign each region a numeric value. Their loss measures squared differences between those assigned values and the original matrix entries. The goal is to summarize a large matrix while preserving the ability to evaluate these trees accurately.

The authors construct a coreset: a small summary whose loss approximates the full matrix's loss for every tree with the specified number of leaves. The approximation is multiplicative, controlled by an error parameter. The abstract also states that optimizing a tree on the summary yields a near-optimal tree for the original matrix.

The construction connects machine-learning decision trees to partition trees from computational geometry. It works for every input matrix, takes O(Nk) time, and produces a summary polynomial in k log(N)/ε. Experiments with sklearn and LightGBM report speedups of up to tenfold for random forests and parameter tuning while maintaining similar accuracy. These empirical gains accompany a uniform theoretical loss-preservation guarantee.
neurips-2021-coresets-for-decision-trees.tldr: Provably small matrix summaries preserve decision-tree losses and deliver up to tenfold empirical speedups while retaining similar accuracy.

paragraphs: Documents communicate through layout as well as words. Tables, graphs, lists, and infographics create varied reading conditions, making document understanding a challenging evaluation problem. This paper introduces Document Understanding Evaluation, or DUE, to provide a shared benchmark for assessing systems across these kinds of documents.

DUE combines existing datasets with reformulated ones and focuses on end-to-end capabilities in realistic scenarios. It includes visual question answering, key information extraction, and machine reading comprehension across different document domains and layouts. Bringing these tasks together gives researchers a common evaluation resource for several distinct demands placed on document-understanding systems.

The authors also establish systematic baselines using recent layout-aware language-modeling methods and analyze challenges in the available datasets. They release both the benchmark and reference implementations. The contribution therefore includes the evaluation tasks and working comparison systems, helping researchers quantify progress in a field where the lack of a commonly accepted benchmark had made comparisons difficult.
neurips-2021-due-end-to-end-document-und.tldr: DUE provides shared tasks and reference systems for evaluating end-to-end understanding of documents with rich, varied layouts.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can be sensitive to optimizer choice, training settings, and schedule length. This paper investigates whether part of that difficulty comes from the first image-processing stage. The authors conjecture that the usual patchify stem, which combines a large convolution kernel with a large stride, contributes to unstable optimization.

They replace that stem with a small stack of 3×3 convolutions using stride two. Most of the computation in the resulting transformer remains identical to the original design, allowing the study to focus on how early visual processing affects training. The comparison examines both sensitivity to optimization settings and final accuracy.

The convolutional stem substantially improves optimization stability and raises peak ImageNet-1k top-1 accuracy by about 1–2% while maintaining computational cost and runtime. Improvements appear across the tested model sizes and dataset scales, from ImageNet-1k to ImageNet-21k. These findings motivate the authors' recommendation to use a lightweight convolutional stem for vision transformers in the investigated regime.
neurips-2021-early-convolutions-help-tra.tldr: Replacing a vision transformer's patchify stem with small convolutions improves training stability and accuracy at comparable computation and runtime.

paragraphs: Distributed training requires machines to exchange gradient information, and compressing those messages can reduce communication costs. Compression also introduces errors that can slow convergence or cause divergence. Error compensation, also called error feedback, is a technique for addressing those errors, but its compatibility with acceleration had remained unresolved.

This paper develops an accelerated method for compressors satisfying a specified contraction property. That class includes biased compressors such as TopK and RandK, as well as appropriately scaled unbiased compressors. The distinction matters because biased compression creates particular difficulties for theoretical analysis of error-compensated optimization.

The authors propose an error-compensated version of loopless Katyusha and prove an accelerated linear convergence rate under standard assumptions. Numerical experiments show that it converges in substantially fewer communication rounds than earlier error-compensated algorithms. The result establishes that acceleration and error-compensated compression can coexist within the studied conditions, connecting reduced message sizes with fewer rounds of distributed communication.
neurips-2021-error-compensated-distribut.tldr: An error-compensated loopless Katyusha method achieves accelerated convergence under stated assumptions and reduces communication rounds in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: The Bayes error rate describes the smallest classification error achievable for a fixed data distribution. Estimating it can help characterize a task's inherent difficulty, but evaluating such estimates on real data is challenging because the true distribution and error rate are unknown. Earlier comparisons therefore commonly relied on synthetic datasets.

FeeBee creates a way to study estimators without knowing the original Bayes error rate. It injects controlled amounts of label noise and evaluates estimators across several noise levels. A theoretical result describes how the Bayes error evolves, providing a basis for assessing estimator behavior as the data are altered.

The authors implement seven multiclass estimators and study them on six computer-vision and natural-language datasets. Their analysis examines practical concerns including computational demands, sample requirements, and sensitivity to hyperparameters. The framework identifies strengths and weaknesses of individual estimators and is designed to accommodate future ones. Its contribution is a principled comparison procedure for realistic datasets with unknown underlying distributions.
neurips-2021-evaluating-bayes-error-esti.tldr: FeeBee uses controlled label noise and theoretical guidance to compare Bayes error estimators on real datasets with unknown distributions.

paragraphs: Garments have highly variable, deformable three-dimensional shapes, yet most originate from collections of flat fabric pieces. This paper uses that relationship to build a synthetic dataset pairing 3D garments with their sewing patterns. Such structural information could provide useful prior knowledge for garment modeling and reconstruction.

The method combines a flexible description format for parameterized sewing-pattern templates with an automated pipeline that generates garment models. It requires little or no manual intervention during generation. The pipeline also creates corrupted mesh versions that imitate artifacts from 3D scanning, adding examples with imperfections relevant to working with scanned shapes.

Using this process, the authors produce more than 20,000 garment design variations from 19 base types. Seven types are specifically designed to evaluate generalization across sewing-pattern topologies, allowing evaluation to address changes in pattern structure. The main contribution is both the paired dataset and a generation method that supports research into the relationship between flat construction patterns and their resulting 3D forms.
neurips-2021-generating-datasets-of-3d-g.tldr: An automated pipeline generates over 20,000 synthetic 3D garments paired with sewing patterns, including scan-like corruptions and topology-generalization cases.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning methods typically construct two views of graph data, but differ in their transformations, architectures, and objectives. Those choices are often carefully customized, leaving limited guidance for designing a method for a new task. InfoGCL addresses this problem by examining how information moves through the learning process.

The framework follows the Information Bottleneck principle. It aims to reduce mutual information between the contrasted parts while preserving information relevant to the target task. The authors apply this reasoning both to individual modules and to the complete framework, using task-relevant information preservation as a guide for design.

The paper reports that its framework unifies the recent graph contrastive methods considered in the work. Theoretical and empirical analyses support the approach, and benchmark experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on graph classification and node classification. The contribution combines a shared explanation of existing designs with a framework for constructing graph representations that retain the information needed for downstream prediction.
neurips-2021-infogcl-information-aware-g.tldr: InfoGCL uses information-bottleneck reasoning to unify graph contrastive learning designs and achieves leading benchmark results for graph and node classification.

paragraphs: KeSpeech is a speech dataset covering standard Mandarin and eight subdialects. It contains 1,542 hours of recordings from 27,237 speakers across 34 Chinese cities. Each recording has multiple kinds of labels, including its transcription, speaker identity, and subdialect, supporting several speech-processing tasks within one resource.

Some text samples were recorded in both standard Mandarin and a particular subdialect. These parallel recordings support applications such as converting subdialect speaking style. The large speaker pool also makes the dataset suitable for tasks needing many distinct voices. Recordings collected in two phases create an opportunity to study how human speech varies over time.

The paper describes the dataset's design and provides four baseline systems: speech recognition, speaker verification, subdialect identification, and voice conversion. Its multiple labels also support multi-task and conditional learning. The contribution is a shared resource for studying linguistic variation alongside speaker variation, with reference systems for several uses. The dataset is available free for academic use.
neurips-2021-kespeech-an-open-source-spe.tldr: KeSpeech provides richly labeled Mandarin and subdialect recordings from over 27,000 speakers for multiple speech-processing tasks.

paragraphs: How the brain could learn deep, hierarchical representations remains poorly understood. This paper proposes a learning rule inspired by neuroscience and self-supervised learning. Each layer minimizes its own loss, without requiring error signals to be backpropagated either within that layer or between different layers.

Weight updates follow a local Hebbian rule. They depend on activity before and after a synaptic connection, predictive input to dendrites, and modulation factors broadcast identically to large groups of neurons. This specifies the information the proposed updates use, connecting the learning mechanism to biological constraints rather than requiring conventional error propagation through the network.

The method adapts contrastive predictive learning to a causal biological setting involving saccades, the rapid movements that shift gaze. Networks trained with the resulting local, self-supervised rule develop deep hierarchical representations of images, speech, and video. The findings demonstrate that this proposed learning mechanism can build such representations across the tested data types, contributing a candidate approach to biologically inspired deep learning.
neurips-2021-local-plasticity-rules-can-.tldr: A biologically inspired local learning rule builds deep image, speech, and video representations without backpropagating errors within or between layers.

paragraphs: Density-ratio estimation compares two probability densities directly. A relative density ratio is a bounded version valued for its stability in tasks such as dataset comparison and outlier detection. This paper addresses the difficulty of estimating it when only a few examples from each distribution are available.

The proposed method learns from related datasets so that it can adapt to a new pair of small datasets. Neural networks extract information about the pair and construct suitable embeddings of individual examples. Within that learned space, a linear model represents the relative density ratio, and its global optimum can be computed in closed form.

That closed-form step supports fast adaptation and is differentiable, allowing training to explicitly minimize expected test error after adaptation to a few examples. The global-optimum claim applies to the linear estimation problem in the embedding space. Experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness for relative density-ratio estimation, dataset comparison, and outlier detection, supporting the use of knowledge from related datasets when observations are scarce.
neurips-2021-meta-learning-for-relative-.tldr: Meta-learned embeddings and a closed-form linear estimator enable relative density-ratio estimation from a few examples using knowledge from related datasets.

paragraphs: Concerns about privacy, bias, and unethical applications have led to prominent machine-learning datasets being withdrawn. This paper asks what the subsequent use of datasets can teach researchers about reducing harm. It studies three influential face and person recognition datasets: Labeled Faces in the Wild, MS-Celeb-1M, and DukeMTMC.

The authors analyze nearly 1,000 papers citing those datasets. Their findings identify several ways ethical concerns can arise over time, including derivative datasets and models, changes in technology and society, unclear licenses, and dataset-management practices. This places dataset use and continued management alongside initial collection as relevant parts of understanding potential harm.

The paper concludes by proposing a distributed approach to mitigation that covers the entire dataset life cycle. The idea follows from the range of activities and changes identified in the study: ethical concerns can develop as data are reused and their surroundings change. The contribution is evidence from citation-based analysis that informs a broader conception of dataset stewardship and responsibility.
neurips-2021-mitigating-dataset-harms-re.tldr: An analysis of nearly 1,000 papers motivates distributed dataset stewardship that addresses harms throughout reuse, management, and broader social change.

paragraphs: Predicting the next place someone will visit is difficult when mobility records are sparse. MobTCast addresses this by combining four kinds of context: temporal, semantic, social, and geographical. Its goal is to use these complementary sources of information to improve next-point-of-interest prediction.

A Transformer-based feature extractor processes a user's sequence of visited places together with semantic information, capturing temporal and semantic context. A self-attention module then incorporates social connections. A separate auxiliary branch predicts the next geographic location, adding an explicit location-forecasting task alongside the prediction of which place will be visited.

The two predictions are linked through a consistency loss: the predicted point of interest should lie geographically close to the location predicted by the auxiliary branch. This gives the model an additional relationship to learn during training. In the reported experiments, MobTCast outperforms other state-of-the-art next-place prediction methods. The findings support combining multiple contexts and using geographical agreement to improve the main prediction task.
neurips-2021-mobtcast-leveraging-auxilia.tldr: MobTCast improves next-place prediction by combining contextual information with an auxiliary location forecast and a geographical consistency loss.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning aims to benefit from abundant unlabeled examples when annotations are scarce. One natural strategy is to extend information from labeled observations smoothly across the data. Laplacian regularization expresses this idea, but existing implementations face difficulties, including the curse of dimensionality.

This paper develops a new class of algorithms intended to overcome that dimensionality problem. The approach reveals a broad family of spectral filtering methods within the proposed treatment of Laplacian regularization. It therefore offers a collection of related algorithmic choices for using unlabeled data, organized around a shared mathematical framework.

The authors provide statistical analysis establishing desirable behavior of their estimators and implement them through reproducing kernel methods. They also give computational guidance aimed at making the approach usable with large datasets. The contribution combines a response to the stated dimensionality drawback with analysis and implementation considerations, connecting the statistical motivation for smooth information transfer to methods designed for practical amounts of data.
neurips-2021-overcoming-the-curse-of-dim.tldr: A new family of Laplacian-regularized methods addresses dimensionality difficulties in semi-supervised learning, with statistical analysis and kernel-based implementation guidance.

paragraphs: Large image collections used for pretraining can contain personal information, unclear licensing, and ethically problematic content. PASS explores whether self-supervised pretraining can work well with a more carefully constrained collection. The dataset is unlabeled, excludes images of people, and includes only CC-BY images with complete attribution metadata.

The authors use PASS with self-supervised methods including MoCo-v2, SwAV, and DINO. Because these methods do not require class labels for pretraining, the study examines an alternative to relying on a labeled resource such as ImageNet. PASS also avoids other image types identified as problematic for data protection or ethics.

In transfer-learning experiments, PASS produces downstream performance similar to ImageNet pretraining, including on human-related tasks such as pose estimation. This supports the claim that useful pretraining is often possible with safer data. The authors explicitly state that PASS does not replace every role of existing datasets and is insufficient for benchmarking. Its contribution centers on pretraining and supporting more robust evaluation of pretraining methods.
neurips-2021-pass-an-imagenet-replacemen.tldr: PASS enables self-supervised pretraining on licensed images without people while achieving transfer performance similar to ImageNet in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Rule-based classifiers offer transparent structures, but their discrete rules and parameters make optimization difficult, especially on large datasets. This paper introduces the Rule-based Representation Learner, or RRL, to learn explicit, non-fuzzy rules for both representing data and classifying it. The aim is to combine interpretability with scalable training.

RRL is non-differentiable, so the authors project it into a continuous space and introduce a training procedure called Gradient Grafting. This procedure enables gradient descent to directly optimize the discrete model. They also redesign logical activation functions to improve scalability and allow continuous input features to be discretized as part of end-to-end training.

Experiments on nine small and four large datasets show that RRL outperforms competitive interpretable approaches. The model can also be adjusted to trade classification accuracy against model complexity for different settings. These results support a route to learning expressive discrete rules while retaining the ability to control how complicated the resulting classifier becomes.
neurips-2021-scalable-rule-based-represe.tldr: RRL uses Gradient Grafting to learn scalable, interpretable discrete-rule classifiers with adjustable accuracy-complexity trade-offs.

paragraphs: MRI reconstruction methods are often judged using image-quality measures that do not align well with clinically relevant quantities. SKM-TEA addresses this evaluation gap with quantitative knee MRI data. The aim is to assess reconstruction and analysis through the quality of tissue-related biomarker estimates extracted from their outputs.

The dataset contains about 25,000 slices from 155 anonymized patients, totaling 1.6 TB. It includes raw measurements, scanner-generated DICOM images, manual segmentations for four tissues, and bounding boxes for sixteen clinically relevant pathologies. These complementary data support evaluating several stages of an imaging workflow using the same collection.

The authors provide a framework combining quantitative MRI parameter maps, reconstructed images, and dense labels to measure biomarker-estimation quality. They use it to benchmark state-of-the-art reconstruction and analysis baselines. The contribution is an evaluation resource connecting technical image-processing outputs to clinically informed quantitative measures, supporting research across reconstruction, segmentation, and detection rather than judging reconstructed images solely by their appearance.
neurips-2021-skm-tea-a-dataset-for-accel.tldr: SKM-TEA pairs knee MRI measurements and detailed labels with a framework for evaluating reconstruction and analysis through quantitative biomarker estimates.

paragraphs: Unlabeled Principal Component Analysis addresses a data matrix whose column entries have been shuffled by permutations. The problem is to recover its underlying low-rank structure despite those disrupted correspondences. Here, unlabeled refers to the missing alignment of entries caused by shuffling.

Using algebraic geometry, the authors establish that the minimum-rank matrices consistent with the observed data are row permutations of the ground-truth matrix. They characterize the solutions through polynomial equations. This gives the recovery problem a precise algebraic foundation while retaining the ambiguity associated with a common permutation of rows.

For the practically relevant case where only a fraction of the data is permuted, the paper proposes a two-stage pipeline. Outlier-robust PCA first estimates the original column space; unlabeled-sensing methods then use that space to restore permuted data. Experiments involving synthetic data, faces, and educational and medical records indicate potential applications in data privatization and record linkage. The work combines an algebraic characterization with a practical recovery procedure.
neurips-2021-unlabeled-principal-compone.tldr: UPCA studies low-rank recovery from column-wise shuffled data and proposes a two-stage recovery pipeline for partially permuted matrices.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents can solve complex individual control tasks, but adapting quickly to new tasks remains difficult. Unsupervised reinforcement learning explores whether pretraining with self-supervised intrinsic rewards can prepare agents for later learning. URLB provides a common benchmark for comparing methods built around that idea.

The benchmark separates evaluation into two phases. During pretraining, the agent does not receive the downstream task's external rewards. During adaptation, it receives extrinsic rewards for the task it must learn. This structure makes the transition from general preparation to task-specific learning central to the evaluation.

Built on the DeepMind Control Suite, URLB contains twelve continuous-control tasks across three domains. The authors provide open-source implementations of eight leading unsupervised reinforcement-learning methods. These baselines make progress but do not solve the benchmark. The findings establish a shared challenge for evaluating adaptation, while the common tasks and implementations support comparison and further development of methods intended to produce more broadly useful agents.
neurips-2021-urlb-unsupervised-reinforce.tldr: URLB standardizes reward-free pretraining and rewarded task adaptation, revealing remaining challenges across twelve control tasks and eight implemented methods.
